div.p: This digital edition presents three related texts from the Ella Evanson Scrapbooks held in University of Washington Special Collections: Ella Evanson’s “Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda” and “The Little Professor,” and her student Tooji’s essay “My Ambition.” Produced in Seattle in the early 1940s, these texts emerge from the wartime classroom of Washington School, where Evanson taught students from diverse racial backgrounds. As Yoon K. Pak argues in Wherever I Go, I Will Always Be a Loyal American , Seattle’s Japanese American schoolchildren experienced a painful contradiction between democratic citizenship education and the racial exclusion authorized by Executive Order 9066. Read together, the three documents in this edition show how children’s literature and student writing were shaped by the historical context of the imminent forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans from the West Coast.

Our edition treats these texts not only as literary or educational documents, but also as social and archival artifacts. “Ming Chin” and “The Little Professor” fictionalize students’ lives through children’s perspectives, while “My Ambition” preserves the voice of a Japanese American student whose aspirations resonate with the fictional figure of Toji in Evanson’s stories. Although this relationship cannot be confirmed with certainty, the similarity between Tooji and Toji invites readers to compare Evanson’s representation of her students with a student’s own self-presentation. Frank Abe and Tamiko Nimura’s We Hereby Refuse: Japanese American Resistance to Wartime Incarceration and Stephen Fugita and Marilyn Fernandez’s Altered Lives, Enduring Community help frame our edition’s attention to Japanese American agency, memory, and community under wartime incarceration.

Our editorial approach is primarily diplomatic. We preserve original spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and historically charged language rather than modernizing or sanitizing the documents. We also use TEI markup to connect fictional characters, real students, places, and historical events through notes and indexes. This apparatus helps readers confront the historical tensions of the texts while also recognizing their value as records of wartime student experience and local Asian American history in Seattle.

div.note: “Japs” This pejorative word reflects the strong anti-Japanese sentiment and wartime hysteria that broke out on the Pacific coast after the Pearl Harbor incident. As the Puget Sound area was mobilized for the war, the local Japanese-American community suffered a severe burden, which eventually led to the emptying of Seattle's vibrant Japantown and thousands of residents being forcibly relocated and detained. A student in the story uses this word to show how deeply these geopolitical tensions permeate the daily social dynamics of children in the classroom.See Warren.

Baby Giant Panda Fund During the late 1930s and early 1940s, the acquisition of a live giant panda from China became a major cultural event in American zoos, often accompanied by large-scale public fundraising campaigns initiated by children. The efforts of the students in the story reflect this real historical “panda craze,” and the content announced by the teacher highlights how the outbreak of the Pacific War suddenly ended these trans-Pacific cultural and diplomatic exchanges.See Croke.

Executive Order 9066 Executive Order 9066 was signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 19 February 1942. It authorized the Secretary of War and designated military commanders to establish military areas from which “any or all persons” could be excluded. Although the order did not name Japanese Americans directly, it was enforced primarily against people of Japanese ancestry, leading to the forced removal and incarceration of approximately 120,000 people, many of whom were American citizens.See National Archives.

Washington School Washington School, also known as George Washington School, was a public junior high school in Seattle’s Central District where Ella Evanson taught seventh and eighth grade from 1928 until her retirement in 1956. The school served students from Japanese American, Chinese American, Jewish, African American, and white families, and it was associated with democratic ideals and racial tolerance. This setting is important for understanding how Evanson’s classroom writings combined progressive educational values with the racial tensions of wartime Seattle.

Tooji and TojiThe name Tooji, used by the student author of “My Ambition,” closely echoes Toji, the fictional Japanese American pupil who appears in Evanson’s classroom stories. This similarity suggests a possible relationship between the student essay and Evanson’s fictional representation, though the connection cannot be confirmed with certainty from the available materials. Reading the student essay alongside the stories allows readers to compare Evanson’s representation of her students with a student’s own self-presentation.
